 Multicolour 3D printing used to be an expensive business. But that’s changing. Several firms are bringing out capable budget models, and the latest to impress us is the Elegoo Centauri Carbon 2 .
 Our reviewer, who’s tested many of the best 3D printers over the last decade, found it easy to use, beautifully built and capable of some of the smoothest results he’s had from an FDM machine.
 Even at full price, it’s cheaper than the Creality K2 Pro. Now Amazon has dropped it from $424.97 to $401.28 , a small yet significant saving.
 Elegoo Centauri Carbon 2: was $424.97 now $401.28 at Amazon This enclosed CoreXY printer can take up to four spools at once, making multicolour prints simple to set up. It calibrates itself, handles a wide range of filaments and delivers sharp, consistent results.
 View Deal 
 Our favourite feature is the Canvas system, which lets you load up to four reels of filament. Our reviewer found it all very quick and easy to load. If your spool has an RFID chip, you just hold it up to the side of the unit and the printer sets everything automatically. When you open a multicolour file, a setup window lets you choose which spool goes where.
 The Centauri Carbon 2 uses a CoreXY design for printing speeds of up to 500mm per second, with a respectable 256 x 256 x 256mm build volume. Our reviewer printed a one-piece fidget toy with moving parts, which came out silky smooth.
 The main drawback is size: with the spools on the side and a waste chute at the back, you’ll need plenty of space around it. Otherwise, this a great value, especially at this discounted price. Read our full Elegoo Centauri Carbon 2 review for more details.

 Prusa’s Core One+ is the 3D printer that changed the way our expert changed prints and thinks about 3D printing. Scoring the full 5 stars in our review, and an Editor's Choice award, he ran it for weeks without a single misprint. And the speed outclasses other multi-filament 3D printers.
 So, I was excited to see the Core One+ for $999 in Prusa's early Black Friday sale (or £919 in the UK). Instead of cutting the price, Prusa is bundling the printer with hundreds of dollars worth of free stuff, including free filament and an OpenPrintTag upgrade.
 • Best for: Professionals and engineers rapidly prototyping models.
 • Why we like it: This is an exceptional 3D printer for serious users. We particularly liked the workshop-style design, which makes it a better fit for many business uses.
 • What you need to know: The Core One+ has a smaller build area than the Core One, but shows improved speed and accuracy compared to other machines of its kind like the Bambu Lab H2C.
 Prusa Core One+ Assembly Kit: $999 at Prusa This early Black Friday deal bundles together just about the best 3D printer we've ever tested alongside free 1kg filament, four new models, a Prusa OpenPrintTag upgrade, an extended warranty, and $50 voucher for upgrading the machine further. Worldwide shipping is free. A pre-assembled version is available for a higher price. 
 UK bundle: now £919 
 Read more Read less ▼ 
 View Deal 
 Why we recommend it
 The Core One+ is a fully enclosed CoreXY 3D printer. It has active chamber temperature control, a 250 x 220 x 270mm build volume and is capable of printing with PLA, PETG, TPU, PC and nylon.
 The second-generation model builds on the first-gen machine's success with redesigned heatbed mounting and an integrated nozzle wiper. It also has new GT1.5 belts to reduce surface artefacts, which means smoother-looking surfaces with fewer visible repeating patterns.
 We recently tested the Gen 2 and were completely blown away - it earned a five-star review and our Editor’s Choice award. Our expert Alastair was particularly enamoured with its multi-material printing capability, and he loved its speed and reliability, even saying it “changed the way I think about printing”.
 The rig ran continuously for three weeks without a single reprint following its initial calibration, and its offline operating options and repairable design also impressed.
 One thing to note: the eight-tool INDX system mentioned in our review is an optional extra, not a standard addition to the CORE One+, and it costs $949 to add to your configuration.
 Prusa's Black Friday deal includes a $50 voucher that can be used toward an INDX tool-changing system.
 For more top performers, check out our guide to the best 3D printers . 
 Price Context & Historical Value
 All of Prusa’s Black Friday bundles offer plenty of value, so they’re great options if you’re already considering investing in a Prusa device.
 The filament, extended warranty, and INDX voucher are particularly useful. They give you a good basis for immediate printing, protect you from any issues for a longer period of time, and empower you to expand your work as you get more confident with the device.
 However, because this isn’t a standard price cut, it’s worth doing a little digging. Weigh up whether you’ll actually use all of the included extras so you can get maximum value out of the deal, and compare the purchase price against competing devices - other units might have price cuts that are better suited to your requirements.
 Should you buy it?
 ✅ Buy the Prusa Core One+ 3D printer if... 
 You want a reliable, enclosed 3D printer with excellent build quality, a repairable design and plenty of upgrade potential. The Black Friday extras make the package particularly attractive if you'll use the additional filament, extended warranty and Prusa Academy courses.
 ❌ Skip the Prusa Core One+ 3D printer if... 
 You want a substantial upfront price reduction. The Black Friday promotion adds value through bundled extras, not with a discount. If you don't need those extras, you may find better value elsewhere.

 Having had the H3C on the workbench for the last month, I still feel like I have only just scraped the surface of what’s possible. The big innovations here are the ability to print with different nozzle sizes, and while this still feels like a technology in development, the potential is obvious. However, as I built a pair of speakers with PLA outer walls and dampening TPU infill, the technical potential demonstrated the next step in 3D printing.

 It was inevitable that there would be a successor to the Bambu Lab H2C , which was no small machine; however, the Bambu Lab H3C takes scale and ability to the next level, although the innovative Vortek Hotend Change System is no more.
 Like the H2C, there’s the multi-tool functionality, but as you’ll see from the images, the system is all new, with dedicated tools in the Swaptek Tool Changer rather than the Vortek hotend-changing system, so something closer to the Bondtech INDX tool changers.
 An interesting update is the ability to print with different-sized nozzles, so a fine 0.2 mm for fine detail, going to a 0.8 mm for infill and areas where speed is preferable to fine finishes. What I have discovered through the month that I’ve had the printer so far is that this is an evolution of the 3D printing process, refining the techniques and while this technology and its application are still being ironed out, the full potential is apparent.
 Latest Videos From TechRadar 
 Watch full video here: 
 Adding to the multi-diameter printing is the advanced TPU handling. This essentially enables you to print with thicker 2.85 mm filament using the PrintTool hotend. As the filament is thicker, it supports softer TPU, and again, there’s a learning process behind its use. It’s not quite as simple as popping it in and letting it go, but it is a step in the right direction.
 Sitting on top of the machine is the new AMS 3H filament management system that holds up to nine filaments, with two slots enabling integrated drying and bypass feeds for specialist materials.
 I’ll admit, as the boxes kept arriving and the H3C started to take shape on the workbench, the machine did seem to dominate the space. However, after squeezing in the H2C next to it, while the new AMS gives a visual impression of scale, the footprint of the two machines is much the same.
 The big question for me at the start of this test was whether this new machine and design was a direct replacement for the H2C or something altogether new. It certainly initially looks far more complex, but then, as I became more familiar with the machine, the full tool changer design, once assembled, did seem, a little more simplistic and certainly more reliable as I pushed the print times and complexities.

 One point to note is that throughout the test, while I had the machine and seemingly every accessory that I could need to go with it, the actual official machine specifications and final tweaking of the software were still to be released.
 What Bambu did supply was a few test models and an extensive set of instructions about how to tackle each of the main new features. There was also a set of complex models that I used to start the test before deviating to some of my own, and then back to the supplied models to finish the test.
 I’ll cover more of those tests in the performance section, but what interested me was using this printer for a real practical task. This is, after all, a business-class machine, although the price will put this just in range of the keen enthusiast as well.
 The main project for this test was to print and build a set of speakers from Print Your Speakers , with the Supersonic MK3 kit fitting the bill for this test. Essentially, a solid PLA outer with TPU to add damping to the infill, and then a switch of nozzle sizes for the fine detail of the outer wall and a thicker nozzle for the inner walls.
 This is where the learning curve of this machine and the Bambu Lab software really comes into play, and while that learning curve is steep.
 As the test ran on, the potential of this machine started to grow. While multi-filament and tool changer machines now dominate and Bambu Lab’s lead in the field was quickly fading, especially with the Original Prusa CORE One INDX, of which the H3C’s new system bears more than a passing resemblance. But with support for 2.85 mm TPU and multiple other materials, it now pushes them back out in front and truly offers something unique, although there are still a few refinements needed.
 Bambu Lab H3C at Bambu Lab for $2,499 
 Bambu Lab H3C: Price and availability 
 The H3C will be available to purchase from the Bambu Lab website from 3 November 2026, following the official launch. Unlike the H2C, there is just one configuration available at launch, with the AMS 3H and all nine PrintTools included.
 H3C AMS Combo: $2,499 / £2,199
 Combo + PLA Palette + TPU: $2,589 /£2,269
 Combo + PLA Palette + TPU + Bambu Station (Enclosed) + E1 Air Purifier: 
 $3,049 / £2,699
 Combo + PLA Palette + TPU + Bambu Station (Open): $2,799 / £2,469
 Bambu Lab H3C: Design 
 (Image credit: Alastair Jennings) BambuLab H2C specifications
 Print Technology: Fused Filament Fabrication (FFF)
 Build Area: 330 × 320 × 325 mm
 Minimum Layer Resolution: To be confirmed
 Maximum Layer Resolution: To be confirmed
 Dimensions: 493 × 571 × 587 mm
 Weight: 36.28 kg (including AMS 3H)
 Bed: Heated, up to 120°C
 Print Surface: Textured PEI plate
 Software: Bambu Studio
 Materials: PLA, PETG, TPU, ABS, ASA, PA, PC, PPA, PPS and other supported materials
 Print Speed: Maximum toolhead speed of 1,400 mm/s
 The Bambu Lab H3C is a 3D printer on another scale, and whilst it doesn’t look that much larger than the H2C initially, once you start to work with it and try to move it around the workshop, you suddenly realise that its colossal 36.28 kg weight and physical dimensions of 493 × 571 × 587 mm make it more of a two-person lift than something you’re able to handle on your own.
 That would explain why Bambu Lab also sent a special trolley along with the machine, so it’s easy to access and move around the workshop. The issue at the moment is that there are so many 3D printers coming out that my workshop doesn’t have any space, so this will be something that I will manoeuvre the printer onto once I can find a pathway through the workshop to get the two sections to meet.
 As it was, I decided to set this machine up in the photo area, and I’ve already manoeuvred the H2C next to it so that I can do a side-by-side comparison on size and scale, however, again this left little room as the the scale of these machine is rapidly increasing.
 As I first lifted the H3C into position, the two machines looked roughly the same size, but as I started to add the huge new AMS 3H on top, I realised that this was an altogether different proposition.
 As I unpacked the machine, it was obvious that Bambu Lab had taken a completely different direction to multi tool head printing compared with the H2C, and the H3C has something more akin to the INDX tool changer. You can definitely see the similarities. As I went through the initial setup, what was surprising here was just how easy and straightforward it was, and whilst the machine was large, the actual placing of the AMS on top and positioning all of the nozzles wasn’t at all difficult.
 The only thing that you do need to make sure of is that there are nine tools included: eight with 0.4 mm PrintTools for 1.75 mm filament and one dedicated 0.4 mm PrintTool for 2.85 mm filament. Careful reference to the instructions as you’re setting up is essential to make sure that this nozzle goes in the right place.
 Before taking a closer look at this new system, it’s worth pointing out that the AMS 3H is quite an evolution on the AMS 2, sitting on top of the machine and really integrating more closely with the design compared with the add-on box of the AMS 2. This, I know, will please a lot of print farms, which, whilst generally fans of the Bambu Lab machines, find the AMS 2 is often a weak point and the part that they have to replace most often. One point here is that, of those nine slots, there’s a separate section within the rack which enables just two of those nine slots to be actively dried.
 As we’ve seen before, you can also add more AMS units, enabling up to 24-colour printing, up from the nine possible out of the box.
 Once I got everything set up and installed, which, to be honest, didn’t take too long, it was then time to connect the machine to the local network via Wi-Fi 6. As ever, this was as straightforward and simple as with all other Bambu Lab machines. One of the surprises is that a machine of this size and scale, especially aimed at the professional market, doesn’t feature an Ethernet port.
 The other point here is that as soon as it connected, it ran through a series of updates before then going through the calibration process. So, while the machine itself is really well designed and easy to set up, the software updating and full calibration process can take up to an hour, which is slightly infuriating when I was quite excited to see what this machine was capable of doing.
 After the Wi-Fi connection, calibration and everything else had been run through, it was time to connect through the Bambu Studio software, and again, a few clicks through the beta release that we were given, enabled me to connect quickly to the printer.
 However, as always, before running through my own prints and some of those others that had been supplied to fully test out this new machine’s abilities, I ran through the standard test prints on the machine. These are the usual 3D Benchy and variants, alongside scrapers and a few other bits and bobs, as expected. It ran through all of those prints flawlessly, and then it was time to cross over to Bambu Studio.
 Bambu Lab actually supplied some very interesting test models, which I go into in the performance section, but before I went into these multi-filament, multicolour designs, I decided to test out some of my more standard prints. This just enabled me to double-check the calibration and also try out a few different materials.
 There are two built-in 1080p cameras, with an optional Bird’s Eye camera available as well. The chamber heats up to 65°C, with a 120°C heated bed and a 350°C maximum nozzle temperature.
 Leaving the machine just to run through those few prints, I was able to step back and take a proper look at the machine, and it is an evolution of what we’ve seen with the other H series printers, just slightly larger. Again, this is a steel chassis, which gives it structural support and also makes it insanely heavy to lift around the workshop.
 The outer is plastic, with a grey and black exterior that looks stylish, just in the same vein as we’ve seen with the other Bambu Lab hardware. On the front, you’ve got a big viewing window so that you can see what’s going on with the print, and whilst the top-mounted AMS 3H does stop you from looking down into the machine, it's integrated rather than being a separate unit, which I personally really like.
 As we’ve seen before, there’s a really nice 5-inch colour touchscreen, with an 854 × 480 display resolution, and this is very responsive, giving me full access to all the functions and settings. However, it is getting more complex, especially with those nine toolheads. It does take a little bit of extra time just to orientate yourself with all of those different settings.
 Across the front is the main feature of this new 3D printer, obviously the new nine-toolhead rack, and what’s interesting here is that the rack raises and lowers, so if you do want to see what’s going on on the print bed, it’s far easier than with some of the other multiple systems of this style out there. At all times, however, you can see where the influence of the Prusa CORE One INDX version has influenced Bambu Lab’s slight change of direction, although they’ve taken that style of design in a slightly different direction.
 The rack features nine individual PrintTool docking positions, and these all automatically dock with tool alignment and offset compensation. What’s interesting here is that there are dedicated filament paths for each PrintTool, meaning that each works completely independently, and there are integrated filament cutters within the PrintTools, again just to help speed things up. When it comes to the extruder and internal mechanisms, they all use hardened steel, with hardened-steel extruder gears and nozzles rated at HRC 55+.
 As ever, we see a flexible steel build plate, and this is a decent size, with a 330 × 320 × 325 mm build volume enabling you to tackle all sorts of projects, especially with the huge material support this new printer offers.
 Bambu Lab H3C: Features 
 (Image credit: Alastair Jennings) It’s difficult to do a quick run-through of the features because, over the H2C, things have really progressed, and the new Swaptek nine-tool changing system is a real evolution of design. You can’t help feeling it’s heavily influenced by the INDX system that we’ve seen from Bondtech and featured on the latest Prusa CORE One machines.
 However, over that system, there are plenty of changes, and it’s obviously got the Bambu Lab spin, with automatic tool changes that happen in under six seconds. There’s also active preheating that essentially anticipates the upcoming tool changes and heats the next nozzle in advance, making complex models slightly faster to print than on some of those other systems.
 One of the features that I noticed early on, and one of the issues with other systems of this style, is that quite often the tool rack gets in the way of being able to see the print area. However, once that new tool is selected, the tool rack actually retracts upwards so that you get a good clear view of the print area, and it also helps to keep the filament tubes out of the way.
 Feeding all of those nine new toolheads is the redesign of the AMS system, known as the AMS 3H, that manages the filaments in an integrated box that sits on top of the machine. Like the AMS 2, it's a sealed storage option and helps protect the filaments inside from moisture.
 Again, as we’ve seen in the past, it has automatic filament loading and routing that works exceptionally well, and with RFID built in, as long as you’re using Bambu Lab’s own materials, they’ll be automatically recognised and synced with the software, making the whole process that much easier.
 One of the surprises is that only two of those nine slots are actively dried, so if you do have filaments that are more prone to moisture than others, then they should sit in those two. There’s a cover that sits over the top, so it’s pretty easy to see which two those are.
 As ever, there are also expansion options, so if you have other AMS systems and you want to plug them in, the H3C supports additional AMS units for up to 24-colour printing.
 One of the new additions is the FlexFeed extruder that supports both 1.75 mm and 2.85 mm filament, and there’s also a dedicated 2.85 mm filament path for flexible materials such as TPU. While TPU for AMS can just be used directly on the machine, as I discovered when I printed speakers with files from Print Your Speakers, when it came to printing other softer TPU, you have to use one of the bypass feed ports and quickly change part of the installation and feed to the toolheads.
 The first time you do it, it takes a little bit of time and working out, but essentially, the soft TPU needs to go into one of the slots that enables active drying. TPU is hygroscopic and collects water like a sponge, so ensuring that it’s nice and dry before it goes through the system is just going to improve and help with the quality of the print.
 You then feed that through into the 2.85 mm supporting toolhead, but rather than running through the filament feed tube, you bypass the tube, cutting just a small length that goes into the toolhead and then directly into the extruder. This just helps with the smooth movement of the TPU filament through the system. This means that it can actually cope with TPU all the way down to 75A, perfect for some of the projects that Bambu Lab supplied.
 Using TPU in the system is not uncommon, but you still have to reconfigure the system slightly. Bambu Lab has made that slightly easier, and of course, you also have the ability to print with multiple materials and multiple colours.
 But what impressed me the most is that with the Bambu Lab PLA palette, which is a new range of filaments, you can print with CMYKW to enable colour mixing using cyan, magenta, yellow, black and white filaments. The end results, as you’re seeing in some of the sample pictures, are quite amazing, enabling far more colourful and complex prints than has previously been possible.
 But it’s not just about multiple colour-mixing filaments. You can also use a huge amount of engineering materials because of the hardened nozzles and the actively heated chamber, so utilising ABS, ASA, PA, PC and carbon-filled composites is all perfectly possible.
 Further supporting the flexibility over the way you print is that there are multiple nozzle sizes, including 0.2, 0.4, 0.6 and 0.8 mm. But what makes a difference here is that you can optimise it to work using those different nozzles in one print. That means you can speed up the printing of the interior support structure with, say, a 0.6 or 0.8 mm nozzle and get that fine-quality finish on the exterior with a 0.2 or 0.4 mm nozzle. This is something very new.
 There’s also been a range of feature enhancements for speed, with a maximum toolhead speed of 1,400 mm/s and acceleration of 25,000 mm/s². To keep up with that high-speed printing, the hotend flow rate of 40 mm³/s is also impressive, although these run to Bambu Lab’s own test conditions rather than what you’re actually going to see in the real world.
 Something which I haven’t really been able to look at in any depth is the CraftTool support, and we’re starting to see Bambu Lab not only promote their machines for 3D printing but for other craft uses. This is what really made the H2D such an interesting machine. Potentially, in the near future, the CraftTools will enable automatic switching between compatible printing and crafting tools, so there will be blade cutting, drawing and debossing, but I’ll bring you more on that when I’ve been able to look at it properly.
 As I mentioned in the Design section, Bambu Lab and, actually, quite a few of the other manufacturers are starting to take filtration seriously, and here we’ve got the H11 HEPA filter, granulated coconut-shell activated-carbon filter and an integrated chamber exhaust and circulation system. Bambu Lab actually even provided an air filter with the machine, which has been very handy, especially in quite a crowded workshop.
 When it comes to features, the H3C is one of the most feature-packed printers to have come onto the market yet, but with all of those features comes an added level of complexity that could cause issues in the long run, and the only way to discover those is to ensure that, over the month of having this machine, it has been running almost constantly.
 Bambu Lab H3C: Performance 
 (Image credit: Alastair Jennings) As these 3D printers get more complex and the models that they’re able to produce become increasingly more elaborate, mixing not only colours but materials, the time it takes to fully test one of these machines is rapidly increasing.
 Thankfully, Bambu Lab recognises that whilst machines are speeding up, when it comes to fully testing some of those mixed-filament options, it doesn’t just take hours; it takes days for each print to be produced. In order for you to run through all of the test prints provided, including rerouting different filaments, that all takes a considerable amount of time.
 But thankfully, I’ve had this printer for almost six weeks, and through that time, there have only been brief periods where it has remained dormant. Otherwise, filament after filament has gone through, producing everything from pinhole cameras out of carbon-filled filament through to some quite incredible desktop speakers, thanks to the guys at printyourspeakers.com, and of course, the extremely elaborate models that the guys at Bambu Lab provided to test out this printer.
 Before I go into that, I’ll just quickly run through the setup process of the machine, as whilst this machine looks extremely complex, the actual setup process is typically Bambu. Essentially, with the machine arriving in two boxes, the machine and a separate box for the AMS, it only took about half an hour before the machine was sitting proudly on the workbench, looking ready to produce its first print.
 The instructions are pretty clearly laid out, and as you’d expect, the large 5-inch touchscreen gives you all the information you need. Once everything is plugged in and connected, you then simply load the filament, and it’s pretty much set to go. However, as always, that complexity comes with a large extra step.
 First, you download and install the firmware, which all ran through nice and quickly, but then it was on to the full setup calibration. Whilst it doesn’t actually take any involvement from yourself other than clicking a couple of buttons, it does take about an hour, and when you have a machine of this size and potential in front of you, that wait is slightly agonising but unfortunately essential.
 Once the machine had run through its copious amount of checks and all the nozzles had been calibrated, it was time to run through the first set of prints, and here I had three different options. Firstly, those pre-installed on the machine in the 64 GB internal storage; the second was my usual test prints; and the third was the additional files that Bambu Lab had provided to fully test out the system.
 I opted for the quick run of those prints in storage just to check whether the calibration had worked and everything was printing correctly, and sure enough, print after print came off the print bed without issue, mixing the colours beautifully into pretty good-quality standard prints. All of these that I started with initially were PLA and mainly ends of reels from previous reviews.
 Then it was on to my own test prints, and again, the accuracy and precision of the printer really stood out, and I was also impressed with the relative speed. One of the big points here is that the tool-changing system, as I saw with the INDX, vastly increases print speeds when compared with the H2C, which is a machine that I actively always have set up and running.
 The speeds with this new system are again slightly faster. A quick test of those print speeds on the H3C, printing the two-tone tree frog in large, took two hours and three minutes, with about eight minutes taken for the preparation time and the rest on the actual model printing. This compared with almost three hours on the H2C, and whilst it was far faster on the preparation and checks at just under six minutes, the print time was closer to two hours and 50 minutes. Finally, comparing it with the H2D, surprisingly, it put in a similar time to the H2C.
 As I ran through the test, the speed of the machine was the first thing that really stood out, and with a relatively large print bed as well, I was able to print large projects with absolute ease. Support structures went in nice and easily, and I always use PLA support, although as I started to venture into Bambu Lab’s own models, I realised the standard PLA support was just not delicate enough for what was needed, and PVA support, which could be washed away, would have been a better option.
 Through my own models, there were quite a few different projects that I wanted to really give a go. The first was a pinhole camera that I had designed for some lectures and was small. It's a good way to test out dimensional accuracy, as I had to drop in a brass-sheet pinhole lens that I had designed and make it tripod-mountable, with brass inserts used for the screw thread.
 As the box also had to be lightproof, dimensional accuracy due to the fitting and removing of a lightproof back was also essential, and using a carbon-filled filament with solid infill just ensured that the whole box would stay lightproof. I also had to feature a sliding shutter mechanism that would cover the brass aperture, so again, quality of surface printing as well as dimensional accuracy was absolutely essential.
 After running several iterations of the design, I came up with the final product and tested it in the studio with success, producing small prints onto photographic paper through a 0.3 mm aperture. The quality of the print and success of the project just highlighted the first bit of flexibility with this machine and its design.
 The next was to call on somebody with a lot more experience with high-quality and precision engineering 3D design, and the guys at Print Your Speakers provided me with the Supersonic MK3 desktop speaker kit to give this new printer a go. There were several angles that I wanted to fully test that no other printer would be able to do.
 The first was obviously to print speakers using PLA for the outer, but then rather than having PLA infill, I wanted it to be TPU in order to help absorb some of the sound. I also wanted to be able to swap between nozzle sizes, all of which took a little bit of experimentation, and at present this is an area of the systems use that I will have to come back to, as at the moment I haven't had any success. I then tested a straight PLA box against the PLA and TPU mixed box, and the difference in audio quality was apparent, with a far deeper sound from the more advanced material-mix option.
 Having now tried a variety of different materials and options through the machine, I was pretty confident about setting off with some of Bambu Lab’s own models to fully test out its abilities. The first was the FROSTSPINE Dragon Bust 1015, which used a variety of materials and took a while to organise the different materials that were needed into the AMS and configure the system.
 Printing this started to point out the big difference between the old Bambu Lab multi-filament AMS systems and this new iteration. It's far more complex, and along with the printing guides that helped guide you through the setup, there’s definitely a greater skill required to get the most out of this machine.
 It took two or three initial attempts before that model rattled off the print bed, taking several days to complete. I then moved on to the hummingbird frame, which was a simple multi-filament PLA mix, and here I really started to see the full potential, being able to mix the colours to create colours that weren’t directly available from a single filament but only once they were blended together, and the results were spectacular.
 The only thing was that I accidentally used PLA support rather than PVA support, so once the final model printed, which took several days, it was going to be a long process to break away all of that support. The intricacy and delicacy of many of the models that you’re now able to print on this machine far exceed what you’ve been able to do before.
 Through this whole process, the one thing that became apparent was that this is a far more hands-on machine, and there is an obvious learning curve, especially working with all the different toolheads, nozzle sizes, bypass filament feeds and potentially additional CraftTools. This is a very feature-enhanced workshop machine at a price that will appeal to both enthusiasts and professionals.
 (Image credit: Alastair Jennings) Bambu Lab H3C: Final verdict 
 (Image credit: Alastair Jennings) In those six weeks of testing, I feel like I’ve only just started to scrape the surface of what’s possible, but there are several key points that I’ve learnt through this test. The first is that if you just want to get straight into printing, then there are cheaper machines out there which will enable you to do that. So if you only print with up to four filaments, which most people do, then the complexity of this machine might be just a little bit above what you need.
 But then, as you start to embrace all its options and capabilities, and if you’re willing to sit down and learn about how to mix materials, how to use those different nozzle sizes together and obviously all those different filament types, then you have a 3D printer that is really quite different from anything that’s come before and sets the tone for what’s coming up in the future.
 Whilst there are more than passing similarities with the INDX system, what Bambu Lab has done here is to evolve what it had done with its previous multi-filament systems and, with this new option, create something that is far more advanced.
 With that increasing complexity come its own issues, and through the process of this review, I did have occasions where I had to rerun the full calibration as one of the nozzles wasn’t quite sitting right. Then there’s the whole bypass reconfiguration of the filament feed, which does get quite complex, but once you’ve done it once, you basically allocate one toolhead to TPU, still leaving you with eight for all other filaments.
 The options and possibilities for this machine are huge, and through this review, I’ve just been incredibly impressed with the overall quality. Each firmware update has fixed some of the issues that I was having early on, such as the RFID not recognising filament reels and, for some reason, the auto-feed system suddenly not auto-feeding. But after the update, those issues were fixed.
 I also had, as you might be able to see on the speaker set, a slight issue with surface finish, but then that’s because I was experimenting with some of those more advanced features, and this was the first time that I had configured the whole process myself in the software. Later, small models printed with much better quality, but again, this is all part of that learning process. As it stands, this printer is a definite evolution of what’s possible and an exciting glimpse into the future of 3D printing.
 Should I buy the Bambu Lab H3C 3D printer? 
 Buy it if...
 You want to print with multiple materials and nozzle sizes. 
 The H3C enables you to combine different materials and nozzle diameters in a single print, something that would be difficult or impossible to produce on more standard 3D printers.
 You want faster, more efficient multicolour printing. 
 With nine PrintTools and material changes taking under six seconds, the H3C reduces the time swapping filaments.
 Don't buy it if...
 You just want a straightforward 3D printer. 
 The H3C has a steep learning curve, especially when mixing materials and nozzle sizes. For standard PLA printing, there are simpler, cheaper options.
 You have limited space or a tight budget. 
 At £2,199 and over 36 kg, the H3C is a substantial investment unless you'll regularly use its advanced features.

 Bambu Lab has just proven exactly why it remains the most innovative brand on the market when it comes to 3D printing. The all-new H3C pushes boundaries unlike any machine I've used before, blending an exquisite tool-swap design with multi-material compatibility, multi-diameter printing, options for processes like cutting and foil transfer, as well as filament storage and drying, all in one beast of a unit.
 I honestly think Bambu Lab might have single-handedly mastered 3D printing with this mic drop of an announcement . I know that's a bold statement, but I can say with confidence, having tested the H3C for the past few weeks, that nothing else even comes close.

 At this point, we might as well scrap our guide to the best 3D printers and just recommend the H3C from now on.
 Jokes aside, every time the 3D printing community has raised an issue, Bambu has responded with a "hold my beer" like approach to fixing it. Purge waste? Eradicated. Wet filament? Not anymore. Long print times? Cut in half thanks to the H3C and Swaptek technology. I'm not sure what else can be improved.
 VIDEO: A first look at the Bambu Lab H3C 
 Bambu Lab H3C: specs & features 
 Where to begin? The highlights boil down to the new Swaptek tool changer, comprising 9 PrintTools (nozzle + a PTFE tube), each with its own filament path for effortless and speedy colour changes in under 6 seconds.
 You may like

 Not to mention there's the new FlexFeed extruder, which accommodates both 1.75mm filament and 2.85mm filament for super soft TPU like the 75A Bambu Lab spools I've been testing.
 The new AMS 3H is humongous, and has been superbly designed to not only store your filament but dry it too, with 2 dedicated chamber slots. Several of the spool slots also have what the company calls a bypass feed, so using materials that aren't suitable for AMS auto-loading, like TPU, has never been easier (I've got a video on this coming soon).

 The only thing that the H3C is missing is a laser module, but I think that's for the best in this case and not needed for this kind of product. You can always get yourself a Bambu Lab R1 if you want to join the laser cutting club, or check out some of the best laser cutters and engravers out there from brands like xTool and Creality.
 It seems like Bambu is on a mission to conquer the craft space, having launched its first standalone laser this year with the R1, and having recently announced that it's dipping its toe into 3D scanners as well. I'm calling it now: in 2027, there will be a Bambu Lab sticker maker, keyring machine, or some type of mini portable maker.

 The best all-in-one printer should make everyday jobs simpler, whether you're printing shipping labels, scanning important paperwork, copying forms or producing colour photos at home. The right choice depends on what you print and how often: some models prioritise rapid document handling, while others keep ink costs down or deliver stronger photo output.
 Our tested picks cover each of those needs, from the Canon Color imageCLASS MF753Cdw II being a capable all-rounder for most households to low-cost options like the Brother INKvestment MFC-T780DW . There's even the Inkwon Tag , a compact creative printer for stickers and creating custom T-shirts.
 At Tom's Guide, we test each printer for printing speeds, print quality, ink costs and more. Read on to find the model that best matches your workload, budget and must-have features, including scanning, copying and faxing.
 Why you can trust Tom's Guide 
 Printers might not be the most impressive (or interesting) things in the world, but they are supremely useful. To make sure you get the best printer possible, our dedicated reviews team put printers through their paces. That's going to be Nikita Achanta , on the Tom's Guide side, who's been testing consumer electronics for years. Then there are our freelancers, such as Eric Butterfield , who's tested a range of brands.
 These are the tests that we put the printers through so that we can properly evaluate their performance.
 We print stuff. Lots of it. Look, it sounds obvious, but we want to check the print quality and sharpness of the prints alongside print speed and other metrics. They're all important.
 Evaluating the app. If there is one — we want to make sure that the application is useful and easy to operate. That's important, especially if you're going to be frequently changing the print settings.
 Testing network stability. If you're going to be printing over your WiFi network, you want to make sure that the printer is going to work well for it. We test out the printer's network to ensure good connection.
 Checking out the color. We want prints to be nice and colorful, with no washing out or color bleeding. We print a bunch of different documents and images, and check out how it performs with different print media.
 Written by 
 Written by 
 Darragh Murphy 
 Buying Guide Editor 
 With the amount of shipping labels I need printed and documents that need copying for my household, a printer has become a quiet essential for my home. That's why I wanted a simple, do-it-all machine, and I refer to our experts, Nikita Achanta and Eric Butterfield , for all the in-depth recommendations they have to offer. 
 The best all-in-one printers you can buy today
 Why you can trust Tom's Guide
 Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate. 
 The best all-in-one printer overall 
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) 1. Canon Color imageCLASS MF753Cdw II 
 The best all-in-one printer overall
 Our expert review:

 Reasons to buy
 + Rapid print, scan and copy speeds
 + Great print quality
 + Responsive and customizable 5-inch touchscreen
 + Large paper output tray
 + Reasonably priced
 Reasons to avoid
 - Expensive toner
 - Quite heavy
 When it comes down to it, the Canon Color imageCLASS MF753Cdw II is quite simply the only printer you'll ever need. Yes, it can print, scan, copy and fax, but it does it all with a hassle-free setup experience and rapid speeds across the board. When a printer actually gives easy step-by-step instructions on how to fix a paper jam, you know it's a good one.
 In our tests, it delivered a five-page text print job in just 11.31 seconds (26.5 pages per minute) and scanned in color in 6.22 seconds, and that's faster than its inkjet competitors. And this 250-capacity printer (plus an extra 150 prints in the middle section) has quick start-up, too, as our reviewer, Nikita, found it effortless to get up and running, with warm-up times as quick as 14 seconds from off. It isn't just speed, as print quality is consistently sharp and detailed, both in color and black and white, and everyday jobs came out looking just as sharp as they did on our screens.
 Where the MF753Cdw II pulls ahead of inkjet competitors like the more budget-friendly Canon MegaTank Pixma G3290 is in raw speed and features. You get much faster printing and a true all-in-one experience (there's no faxing on it), but running costs are higher if you print in volume. Against the business-class Epson EcoTank Pro ET-5850 , the MF753Cdw II still keeps up on print speed and quality but can’t match those rock-bottom ink costs.
 That’s the main compromise here: the per-page price is higher than what you’ll find with most ink tank printers (around 51 cents per color page and 27 cents per mono print). But not by that much, and that shouldn't put you off grabbing this workhorse. If you want a dependable, fuss-free machine for everyday tasks — letters, homework, invoices, you name it — the MF753Cdw II is the best fit for most households.

 + Duplex printing

 Reasons to avoid
 - Small LCD (not a touch screen)
 - Manual feed slot limited to one sheet
 - Does not make two-sided copies/scans via ADF
 Unless you need faxing in your life, this is the all-in-one printer to grab if you're after a reliable machine for excellent prints. The Brother INKvestment MFC-T780DW stands out largely thanks to its exceptionally low ink costs: just 0.3 cents per black page and 0.94 cents per color page based on our lab testing. That's value you can't ignore.
 In daily use, the T780DW keeps pace with demanding routines. It prints standard text documents at 12.4 pages per minute (ppm) and handles double-sided text at 6.7 ppm. These speeds put it among the fastest inkjets we've tested for both single and duplex jobs, making it reliable for everything from schoolwork to business invoices.
 Print and scan quality are equally reassuring. In our hands-on tests, text and graphics came out crisp and accurate, while color scans preserved detail and clarity.
 The main compromise is its 20-sheet automatic document feeder. While fine for light multi-page copying and scanning, if you've got a large batch of documents, it will take some time to do. That, and there's no USB thumb drive port, and don't expect to make double-sided copies or scans via the automatic document feeder (ADF).
 In any case, for those who want low running costs and easy printing, the Brother MFC-T780DW will fit in nicely with your home or office.

 Whether you're a photographer or just need highly detailed, colorful prints, the Canon MegaTank Pixma G3290 is the all-in-one printer for you. Sure, it may come with fewer additional features, but it excels where it matters: print quality and affordability.
 It's a modest printer; it has just one paper tray and no document feeder, and it's not the speediest option. But for home use, it's an excellent choice. Expect this to deliver reliable, high-quality prints with the versatility to do documents, photos and double-sided print jobs. Speaking of which, those graphic prints and glossy photos will come out with plenty of detail and natural, accurate colors.
 While the Canon MegaTank Pixma G3290 prints at pretty average speeds, it actually excels at double-sided documents. In our testing, it printed single-sided pages at an average of 9.2 pages per minute, but double-sided text documents cranked up to 7.2 pages per minute, the fastest duplex print speed we've recorded of any recent ink tank printers.
 And thanks to its easy setup process, robust wireless support (this thing can print via Wi-Fi or a smartphone app) and low ink costs (we estimate color prints cost roughly 0.9 cents per page, significantly lower than the 1.9 cents per page category average), I recommend the Canon MegaTank Pixma G3290 for anyone seeking an affordable, reliable ink all-in-one printer, especially for photo printing.

 Reasons to avoid
 - Occasional paper feed issue

 If your at-home office needs fast, reliable color printing day in and day out, the Epson EcoTank Pro ET-5850 is just the printer you'll want. In our tests, it handled a six-page mixed color document in just 1 minute and 8 seconds (5.3 pages per minute), nearly doubling the category average, so you won’t be waiting on big print jobs during busy stretches.
Where the XP-8800 really stands out for speedy work prints is its speed with graphics-heavy jobs. Letter-size glossy photos print in 2 minutes and 21 seconds, far outpacing typical inkjets. The three separate paper input trays mean you can keep letter, legal, and specialty papers ready to go, which helps minimize interruptions if multiple people are printing different document types.
 Moreover, you're getting an impressively low ink costs with a device capable of handling more than 3,000 pages per month. During our testing, we found an extremely low per-page cost of 0.4 cents for text pages, and 1.6 cents per color page. The printer can scan, copy and fax, uses dual 250-page paper cassettes and has a 50-sheet automatic document feeder.
 Setup was mostly straightforward, but we did run into some hiccups. Connecting to our network required manually entering a router password (WPS isn’t supported), and the touchscreen flagged network issues before resolving. Once added, using the printer with a Mac was simple, but it’s worth noting you might spend extra time on initial setup and troubleshooting.
If you’re after an all-in-one that keeps pace with high-volume, graphics-rich business tasks and want flexible paper handling, the XP-8800 is a great fit.

 Inkwon Tag is available for $299 (via Kickstarter) 
 Alright, this one's a little different from any other all-in-one printer, as the Inkwon Tag is a one-of-a-kind portable color inkjet printer. Instead of printing, scanning or copying documents or photos, this pocketable printer delivers all the fun stuff — instant photo prints for scrapbooks, heat transfers for creating custom T-shirts, temporary tattoos and even stickers.
 This 4-in-1 portable printer is as tiny as it is light, coming in at 4.1 x 3.8 x 1.7 inches and weighing just 8.2 ounces. Our reviewer, Nikita, has no problems carrying this around in a pocket, as it's actually smaller than the best big phones around today.
 Despite its size, you'll find it boasts surprisingly good print quality, no matter the image. It uses a CMY three-dye-based ink system (no dedicated black ink, though) with a resolution of 600 dpi, making it excellent for small prints of friends and loved ones, designs of your choosing or even screenshots from games. And it's all extremely easy to use, right from setting it up to the very user-friendly app for editing and printing photos.
 It isn't perfect, as it can only handle one sheet of paper at a time, and don't expect it to create any borderless prints. It's also quite a pricey portable printer, coming in at $299, but its ink costs and paper refills are much more value-friendly when compared to its competition, especially from Canon or Instax (plus, they don't offer 4-in-1 portable printer options with sticker or heat transfer capabilities).
 To have a mini, portable printer by your side to instantly create stickers to personalize whatever you want, temporary tattoos for parties, heat transfers for customized T-shirts and Polaroid-like photos, all at low running ink costs? As far as portable all-in-one printers go, the Inkwon Tag is a winner.

There are only 18 sheets of sticker/photo paper out of the box, so you'll need to invest in more, and the Inkwon Tag offers a bit more "all-in-one" versatility, but the Cricut StickerPix Print + Cut is well worth grabbing for all things stickers!

The Brother INKvestment MFC-J995DW bucked the trend of printers gouging you on ink costs by coming with roughly a year's worth of ink (depending on how much you print) pre-loaded in the extra-large ink cartridges, so you get a great price-per-page right out of the gate. On top of that, the Brother INKvestment MFC-J995DW offers solid printing, scanning and copying. But this model is trickier to find these days, and more of the current Brother printers of its kind do just the job for less these days. 
 Read our full Brother INKvestment MFC-J995DW review 
 View Deal 
 Brother MFC-L2750DW XL: $799 at Amazon (★★★★☆½) 
The Brother MFC-L2750DW XL is the best multifunction laser printer we've reviewed in years for everything but color prints. Every print is sharp and clean, and it's packed with features including a quick ADF, fast duplex printing and copying, fax capability, and a second paper tray. But this is one pricey machine!
 Read our full Brother MFC-L2750DW XL review 
 View Deal 
 Canon Pixma TR8620: $215 at Newegg (★★★★☆) 
Looking for another photo printer option? The Canon Pixma TR8620 is a fantastic shout that offers plenty of office features, from scanning and faxing to a 20-page ADF, a duplexer for two-sided printing, and two paper trays for keeping two types of paper at the ready. But that extra ink cartridge does bump up the cost of ink. 
 Read our full Canon Pixma TR8620 review 
 View Deal 
 Best All-In-One Printer: Frequently Asked Questions 
 (Image credit: Nikita Achanta / Tom's Guide) Which all-in-one printer has the lowest running costs?
 Ink-tank printers, a type of Inkjet, usually offer the lowest running costs because their refill bottles deliver far more pages than conventional cartridges. In our guide, the Brother INKvestment MFC-T780DW is the best-value option for home or light-office use, while the Epson EcoTank Pro ET-5850 pairs very low per-page costs with the capacity and features needed for heavier business printing. You should compare current cost-per-page figures with your expected print volume, not just the printer’s upfront price.
 Should I buy an inkjet or laser all-in-one printer?
 Choose an inkjet if you print colour graphics or photos, want a lower upfront price or value the low ongoing costs of an ink-tank model. Choose a laser all-in-one if your priority is fast, sharp text documents and a responsive office workflow. The Canon Color imageCLASS MF753Cdw II is our top pick, as it's a fast laser workhorse, whereas the Canon MegaTank Pixma G3290 is the stronger fit for photo printing.
 Do I need an all-in-one printer with an automatic document feeder?
 An automatic document feeder (ADF) is worthwhile if you regularly scan, copy or fax multi-page documents, as it feeds the sheets for you instead of requiring one page at a time on the scanner glass. It matters less for occasional household printing or photo-focused use. Also check its capacity and whether it supports double-sided scanning: an ADF does not automatically mean both sides can be scanned in one pass.
 Can an all-in-one printer scan and copy double-sided documents?
 Some can, but not every all-in-one printer with an ADF supports automatic double-sided scanning or copying. Do not confuse duplex printing with duplex scanning: a printer may print on both sides of a sheet while still requiring you to turn over originals when scanning or copying. Check the model’s specifications before buying; the Brother INKvestment MFC-T780DW has an ADF but does not support duplex scanning or copying through it.
 Can I print from my phone or tablet using an all-in-one printer?
 Many current all-in-one printers support wireless mobile printing through a manufacturer app, Apple AirPrint or another built-in service. The Canon MegaTank Pixma G3290 , for example, supports Wi-Fi and printing through a smartphone app. Before buying, confirm that the printer works with your phone or tablet, operating system, preferred app and network setup. Some features may require the device and printer to be on the same Wi-Fi network.
 How to choose the best all-in-one printer for you 
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) Not sure which all-in-one printer to buy? No worries, I'm here to help.
 Obviously, you want a printer that performs well, so all of our reviews and rankings discuss a printer's output quality and speed, but there's more to an all-in-one printer than just how quickly it can crank out documents.
 Price: All-in-one printers sell for as little as $60 (£45/AU$90) for inkjet models and $150 (£170/AU$200) for laser printers, with high-end models costing hundreds of dollars but offering better print quality, durability, and features. And don’t forget ink and toner, which can range from 1 to 5 cents per page for basic documents (photos will cost more).
 Inkjet or Laser: Next, it helps to determine whether you need an inkjet or a laser printer . Inkjet printers are generally better suited to producing the full range of colors, making them better suited to printing graphics and photos. Laser printers can quickly produce professional-looking text documents, often at a lower cost per page.
 Home or Office: Home and office printers differ greatly in their handling of large print volumes. Some printers are built to offer great quality and value for the home user who prints a few pages a week, while others are built for busy offices where multiple users print dozens or hundreds of pages every day. Find the one that’s right for you to avoid paying for features you don’t need.
 Use case: Additional use cases, like photo printing, are addressed in our selections above, while specific features are discussed in every printer review we do. Portable printing is another niche area where the right printer can make a world of difference.
 Operating expenses: Finally, consider the cost per page. Whether it’s using ink cartridges or toner, printers cost money over time. Check our reviews for a breakdown of the costs to print individual pages as a good measure of how expensive operating costs will be over the life of the printer.
 Some companies even offer subscription services that save you money while sending you ink just in time to replace that empty cartridge. Learn more in our article HP Instant Ink vs. Canon vs. Epson: Are ink subscriptions worth it? 
 How we test the best all-in-one printers 
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) To help you find the best all-in-one printer, we put each model through an extensive range of printer tests , including timed prints of text, mixed text and graphics and color photos. The resulting prints are carefully examined for errors and issues, and compared with samples from other printers to determine the print quality.
 We time every test print to see how quickly the machine handles document printing, and closely examine the finished product to determine how well different printing tasks are handled.
 We also test the scanning and copying functions of the printer, timing how quickly it captures a page and comparing the results to the original images to determine how well it captures color and detail.
 To measure the cost of owning and operating a printer, we look at the current street price of ink refills and the estimated number of pages that each cartridge can produce, and calculate the cost for printing a single page.

 Selecting your first 3D printer sets the tone for your journey into a new hobby or even a small business. With so many competing brands on the market, each backed by a passionate fan base, choosing the right beginner 3D printer can feel overwhelming. Spend a few minutes in any online forum, and you’ll quickly see the divide: a machine praised as a game-changer by one group can be dismissed as a steaming pile of garbage by users who had a bad experience.
 It doesn’t have to be this way. We’re here to cut through the rhetoric and brand loyalty to provide practical, experience-based guidance. We were beginners once ourselves, starting out on manually leveled machines running bare-bones firmware, long before Wi-Fi, touchscreens, or onboard cameras were standard. If we had to start over today, these are the beginner 3D printers we’d choose without hesitation.

 A 3D printer for a child has to clear a different bar from one for an adult: the child has to be able to run it, and a parent has to be comfortable with it running in the house. Start with age, because the guides we researched agree on three bands. Children of about 5 to 8 are best served by a toy-style printer such as the Toybox Alpha Three, which prints from a phone or tablet app's catalog with no slicer, no bed leveling and no heated bed. From about 9, a self-calibrating printer such as the Bambu Lab A1 mini is usable with an adult nearby, and it will keep a child busy for years. Teenagers of about 12 and up can step up to an enclosed machine such as the Flashforge Adventurer 5M Pro or a hands-on budget model such as the Creality Ender-3 V3 SE.
Next, decide how much the enclosure matters. Every printer here has a nozzle above 200°C. Open-frame printers (the A1 mini, A1 and Ender-3 V3 SE) leave it and the moving bed exposed, so younger children need supervision and the printer should sit out of reach of siblings and pets. The Adventurer 5M Pro closes everything behind a door and filters its air with HEPA and activated carbon; the Toybox keeps its small print area enclosed and has no heated bed at all.
Then look at how a print actually starts, because that decides whether a child uses the printer on their own. The Toybox and the two Bambu Lab printers print ready-made models from a phone app with one tap. The Adventurer 5M Pro works from its touchscreen and app, with a desktop slicer for custom models. The Ender-3 V3 SE has no Wi-Fi: every print is sliced on a computer and carried over on a microSD card, which suits a teen who wants to learn the process and frustrates a younger child.
Finally, weigh build volume against how long the printer should last. The Toybox's 75 × 80 × 90 mm area prints small toys, and reviewers expect children to outgrow it by about age 10 or 11. The A1 mini's 180 mm cube covers most kids' projects, while the A1's 256 mm cube handles helmets and cosplay parts.  Questions, answered
 What age is right for a child's first 3D printer? The guides we researched split it into three bands. Children of about 5 to 8 do best with a toy-style printer like the Toybox Alpha Three, which prints from an app catalog with no setup. From about 9, a self-calibrating printer like the Bambu Lab A1 mini is usable with an adult nearby, and teenagers of about 12 and up can handle an enclosed printer like the Flashforge Adventurer 5M Pro or a hands-on model like the Creality Ender-3 V3 SE. Supervision matters more than the number: every printer here has a nozzle that runs above 200°C.
 Is an enclosed 3D printer safer for kids? An enclosure keeps small hands away from the hot nozzle and moving parts while the printer runs, which is why several kids' guides recommend one for children under 12. The Flashforge Adventurer 5M Pro is fully enclosed and filters its air, and the Toybox Alpha Three has an enclosed print area and no heated bed. The Bambu Lab A1 mini, A1 and Creality Ender-3 V3 SE are open-frame, so keep them out of reach of younger children and supervise their use.
 Are 3D printer fumes safe for children? Print PLA, the plant-based filament every pick here supports and every guide we researched recommends for kids; it gives off far fewer fumes than ABS or ASA. Run the printer in a ventilated room rather than a closed bedroom where possible. The Adventurer 5M Pro adds HEPA and activated-carbon filtration, which is useful if the printer will sit in a bedroom or study. Avoid resin printers for children because of their liquid resin and alcohol cleanup.
 Does a kids' 3D printer need a computer? Not for most picks here. The Toybox Alpha Three prints from a phone or tablet app, and the Bambu Lab A1 mini and A1 print MakerWorld models from the Bambu Handy app or their own touchscreens. The Flashforge Adventurer 5M Pro works from its touchscreen and app, though custom models go through a desktop slicer. The Creality Ender-3 V3 SE is the exception: it has no Wi-Fi, so prints are sliced on a computer and loaded on a microSD card.
 Will my child outgrow a Toybox? Probably by about age 10 or 11, according to GeekBitz. The Toybox Alpha Three's 75 × 80 × 90 mm build area limits it to small toys, and it prints PLA only. If your child is already 9 or older, or likely to stick with the hobby, the Bambu Lab A1 mini is a better long-term buy: its 180 mm cube holds about ten times the Toybox's volume and it can add four-color printing later.

 Conventional 3D printers require adult supervision because they combine heated components, moving mechanisms, electrical equipment, and material emissions. A child-friendly label or toy-oriented catalog is not proof that a printer can run unattended in a child’s room.
 Safety rules for a family 3D printer
 An adult should perform initial assembly, calibration, maintenance, and any work involving the hot end or heated bed.
 Run a filament printer in a well-ventilated area, not beside a child’s bed or in a small, poorly ventilated room.
 Keep hands, hair, clothing, and tools away from moving parts and heated surfaces.
 Do not let children remove stuck prints or touch the nozzle and bed while those components are hot.
 Use the material recommended by the manufacturer, generally beginning with PLA for the reviewed printers that support it.
 Keep children away from scrapers, cutters, replacement nozzles, electrical connections, and other maintenance tools.
 Use a printer’s camera or remote monitoring features as supervision aids, not as substitutes for an adult being responsible for the machine.
 The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s 3D-printing research says 3D printing can release volatile organic compounds and ultrafine particles. EPA identifies children as a potentially vulnerable population and discusses controls including lower-emission materials, enclosures, ventilation that captures chemical emissions, and reducing time near a running printer.

 Can you sell a home-printed object as a children’s toy? 
 A home-printed object intended to be sold or marketed as a children’s toy may be subject to applicable children’s-product safety rules, testing, and certification requirements.  That distinction is different from printing a decorative model for personal use. Families should not assume that a successful print, a PLA label, or a model downloaded from the internet establishes compliance for a product offered to children.

Teachers should not need a soldering iron or a firmware flash just to start a print.
 Safety is not just about an enclosure. It also means stable firmware, thermal runaway protection, and a heated bed that does not stay dangerously hot after a print. PLA is the right starting material for most classrooms. It prints at lower nozzle temperatures around 200°C and usually does not require a heated bed, though a warm 50°C bed improves adhesion. Our 3D printing materials guide compares PLA, PETG, and ABS. Avoid ABS and uncured resin for elementary-age kids unless you have serious ventilation and supervision. A small spill of molten plastic is manageable. Breathing styrene fumes is not. Start with PLA and only move up if a project demands it.
 Price matters for schools buying five or ten units. A $199 printer becomes a $1,990 classroom expense before you add spare nozzles, build plates, and filament.  Frequently Asked Questions # 
 Are 3D printers safe for kids? 
 Most modern 3D printers are safe with supervision. An enclosed frame, automatic bed leveling, and thermal runaway protection reduce risks. Keep small children away from hot nozzles and moving parts, and always use PLA for elementary-age kids.
 What is the best age to start 3D printing? 
 Kids as young as 5 can use a Toybox printer with an adult nearby. Ages 10 and up can handle open-frame machines like the Bambu Lab A1 Mini with basic instructions.
 Do I need an enclosed 3D printer for a classroom? 
 Not always. An enclosed printer is safer for young kids and improves print consistency for PETG. But an open-frame machine on a high shelf with supervision works for older students.
 What filament is safest for kids? 
 PLA is the safest common filament. It prints at lower temperatures and does not require a heated bed. Avoid ABS and resin for young children unless you have strong ventilation and supervision.
 Do students need to know 3D modeling? 
 No. Many printers include pre-sliced models or use apps like Toybox. Students can start with ready-made files and learn Tinkercad or CAD later.
 How much should a school budget for a classroom 3D printer? 
 A good single printer costs $169 to $499. Plan for extra filament, spare nozzles, and a replacement build plate. A $199 printer can become a $300 setup after accessories.

 3D printing is no longer a hobby reserved for engineers and hardcore makers. In 2026, a new generation of affordable, safe, and genuinely easy-to-use printers has made it one of the best STEM activities a family or classroom can adopt. Kids as young as six can design a toy in a browser-based app and watch it materialize an hour later — an experience that teaches spatial reasoning, iteration, patience, and basic engineering thinking better than almost any other at-home activity.

 But not every 3D printer belongs in a child’s hands. Hot nozzles reaching 260 °C, exposed moving parts, fumes from the wrong filament, and tangle-prone spools can turn a fun afternoon into a hazard. This guide walks you through what actually matters when buying a 3D printer for kids, which models we recommend in 2026, and how to set up a printing routine that keeps children safe while they learn.

 What Makes a 3D Printer Kid-Friendly?

 Safety Rules Every Parent Should Enforce

 Final Verdict 
 What Makes a 3D Printer Kid-Friendly?
 Marketing teams love slapping “beginner-friendly” on any cheap printer, but kid-friendliness is a specific combination of hardware design, software, and support. Here are the criteria we use.
 Safety First: Enclosed or Guarded Hot Parts
 The nozzle of an FDM printer runs between 190 and 260 °C, and the heated bed reaches 60–100 °C. A curious finger poked at the wrong moment causes real burns. Fully enclosed printers physically separate children from hot components, while open-frame printers should at minimum keep the gantry behind a clear barrier or sit on a high shelf under active adult supervision. If your child is under ten and will be anywhere near the machine unsupervised for even a minute, an enclosed model is worth the premium. Our dedicated enclosure buyer guide covers retrofit options for open-frame printers.
 Auto-Leveling and One-Touch Setup
 Manual bed leveling is the single most common way beginners ruin their first prints — and it requires judgment a child simply does not have yet. Every printer we recommend below ships with automatic bed leveling. The machine probes its own bed, compensates for imperfections, and starts printing. This removes the most frustrating failure mode and lets kids experience success on their first attempt, which is the whole point.
 Software Kids Can Actually Use
 Tinkercad remains the gold standard for children: it is free, browser-based, and built around dragging simple shapes together. Printers that integrate well with it — or ship their own kid-oriented app with a curated model library — massively shorten the path from idea to object. Avoid printers whose only workflow is a professional slicer with dozens of intimidating settings. For parents who eventually want more control, our slicing software guide explains the upgrade path.
 Noise and Placement
 A printer that sounds like an angry sewing machine will not survive in a family living room or a classroom corner. Look for silent stepper drivers (almost universal in 2026) and read real user reviews about noise. Also consider size: a compact printer fits on a desk where an adult can keep an eye on it, which is safer than a big machine banished to an unsupervised garage.

 The A1 Mini is the printer we recommend most often to parents. It is fast, remarkably reliable, auto-levels, and produces excellent prints straight out of the box with almost zero tinkering. The 180 mm build volume is plenty for toys, figures, and school projects, and its speed means a child’s design is finished in an hour rather than overnight — a huge deal for maintaining a kid’s interest. The optional multicolor system (AMS lite) lets children print multi-colored objects without any manual filament swaps, which is pure magic for younger makers. Print quality is modest compared to enthusiast machines, but for the target age group the experience — browse, tap, print, play — is unbeatable. It is the closest thing to a “toy that makes toys” on the market. See the Toybox 3D Printer for Kids for current bundles, which often include filament packs.

 For around $100–150, the Ender-3 V3 SE delivers auto-leveling, a respectable build volume, and Creality’s mature ecosystem. It is an open-frame printer, so it demands the supervision rules we outline below, but for a family on a tight budget — or a child who has already outgrown a toy-focused machine — it is the best value in entry-level printing. Pair it with a cheap PLA multi-pack like the PLA Filament 1.75mm Multi Color Pack so kids can experiment with color without you worrying about waste.

 FlashForge Adventurer 5M — Best Enclosed Mid-Range Option
 The Adventurer 5M line offers a fully enclosed chamber, quick-swap nozzles, and fast printing in a package that costs far less than pro enclosed machines. The enclosure makes it the strongest candidate for households with younger siblings or for shared classroom spaces where supervision is intermittent. It also handles slightly more advanced materials when your child is ready to move beyond PLA. Current pricing: FlashForge Adventurer 5M 3D Printer .

 MakerBot Sketch Sprint — Best for Classrooms
 For schools, the Sketch Sprint is sold as an education kit: printer, curriculum-aligned lesson plans, filament, and teacher training in one package. Its enclosed design, HEPA filtration, and managed print software are designed around exactly the constraints of a classroom with thirty kids and one teacher. It is overkill for a single family, but for educators it removes months of integration work. Compare education pricing on the MakerBot Sketch Sprint Classroom 3D Printer .
 Check Price on Amazon → 
 Materials: Stick to PLA
 PLA is the only filament families should start with. It prints at low temperatures (190–220 °C), does not require a heated enclosure, warps rarely, produces minimal odor, and comes in every color a child could want, including silk, glow-in-the-dark, and gradient blends. Avoid ABS and ASA around kids — both emit fumes during printing that require ventilation — and skip exotic engineering filaments until your child understands machine operation fully. Our PLA filament buyer guide ranks the brands worth buying in 2026.
 One habit worth building immediately: dry storage. PLA absorbs moisture over time, and damp filament produces brittle, stringy prints that frustrate kids. A simple sealed box with desiccant solves it — see our filament dryers and storage guide for options that cost less than a pizza night.
 Safety Rules Every Parent Should Enforce
 Even the safest printer needs household rules. Print these and tape them next to the machine:
 No touching the nozzle or bed during or right after a print. Both stay hot for ten to fifteen minutes after completion.
 Adult starts the print. Kids can queue jobs from the app; a grown-up confirms the bed is clear and settings are sane.
 Print in a ventilated room. PLA fumes are minimal, but fresh air is free.
 Never leave the printer running overnight until your specific machine has proven itself reliable for a month of supervised use.
 Keep fingers away from belts and gantries while moving. Pinch points are the most common minor injury with open-frame printers.
 A fireproof enclosure like the 3D Printer Enclosure Fireproof Box adds a further layer of protection for open-frame machines placed in busy family spaces.
 Check Price on Amazon → 
 Getting Started: First Projects That Hook Kids
 The fastest way to kill a child’s interest is a failed twelve-hour print. Start small and personal:
 Name tags and keychains — 20 minutes, teaches the design-to-print loop end to end.
 Articulated flexi animals — print-in-place models that move without assembly. Printables and MakerWorld have thousands; kids adore them.
 Replacement parts for their own toys — a broken wheel or lost game piece. This quietly teaches them that 3D printing is a tool, not just a toy.
 Custom cookie cutters — design in Tinkercad, bake the same afternoon.
 Once the basics click, multicolor printing is the natural next step — printing a rainbow keychain or a two-color figure feels like a superpower. Our multicolor printing systems guide explains how the different approaches work and what they cost.
 Maintenance Kids Can Help With
 Involving children in maintenance builds ownership. Age-appropriate tasks: peeling finished prints (with supervision), brushing the nozzle plate when cold, checking filament spools for tangles before a print, and wiping the bed with isopropyl alcohol. Adults handle nozzle changes and any work near hot components. A basic toolkit from our 3D printer tools guide covers everything, and most of it is genuinely usable by a careful ten-year-old.
 FAQ
 What age is appropriate for a 3D printer?
 With a kid-focused machine like the Toybox and adult supervision, age six is reasonable. With a general-purpose printer like the A1 Mini, we recommend ages eight to ten and up, with an adult operating the machine until the child demonstrates consistent, rule-following behavior.
 How much should I spend?
 Between $100 and $300 buys a genuinely good starter experience in 2026. Below that, expect more failed prints and frustration; above it, you are paying for speed and features a beginner will not miss.
 Is 3D printer filament toxic?
 PLA is made from plant starch and is considered the safest common filament, with minimal odor. It is not food-safe in printed form, so printed cookie cutters should be used with a dough barrier or for play-dough only. Never print food-contact items with ABS or ASA.
 Do we need an enclosure?
 For children under ten, or any printer in a shared family space, yes — either buy an enclosed model or add a retrofit enclosure. For older kids in a supervised workshop, an open frame is acceptable with the rules above.
 Final Verdict
 For most families, the Bambu Lab A1 Mini is the best kids’ 3D printer in 2026: reliable enough that failures are rare, fast enough to hold a child’s attention, and supported by an ecosystem that grows with them. Younger children get the purest experience from the Toybox Alpha, classrooms are best served by the MakerBot Sketch Sprint, and budget-conscious families can build a great setup around the Creality Ender-3 V3 SE. Whichever you choose, pair it with PLA, enforce the safety rules, and start with small, personal projects — the printer is the easy part; the habit of designing, printing, failing, and trying again is the real gift you are giving your kid.
